problem: Two of the three options are misspellings ("helmit", "helment").
evidence: Showing learners wrong spellings weakens their memory for the right one (Brown 1988, J Educ Psych 80(4); Jacoby & Hollingshead 1990); dyslexic learners are most affected. Real words test the same visual check.

problem: Children read "Fire is safe to touch." as a printed statement.

problem: The printed sentence advises hiding when lost; an anxious child may keep that idea, and 12 words is long for this level.

fix.prompt: If you are lost, you tell a grown-up you trust.
fix.audio_text: If you are lost, you tell a grown-up you trust.

evidence: Rubric safety wording: the safe choice is to tell a trusted adult (NSPCC). Keeps 6 yes / 4 no in the set.

problem: "the green man" is a UK/Irish term for the walk signal.

fix.prompt: We wait for the green light to cross the road.
fix.audio_text: We wait for the green light to cross the road.

evidence: Rule 12 (local and fair). Same fix as EN-LIS-T03-Q04.

problem: "adds up over time" is an idiom ("adds up" also means a sum) in a 10-word sentence.

fix.prompt: Saving a coin each week gives you more money.
fix.audio_text: Saving a coin each week gives you more money.

evidence: Rule 2: literal language; idioms cost autistic learners and learners with DLD processing time (Vulchanova et al. 2015).

problem: "I wash my hair before dinner" is also a sensible sentence, so "hair" is defensible.
evidence: One defensible answer per item. Same fix as EN-LIS-T09-Q01.

problem: "batter" is a low-frequency word for young readers (and a cricket/baseball player).

fix.prompt: First mix the cake. Then bake the cake. Then blow out the candles.

evidence: Rule 1 (everyday words); the listening version EN-LIS-T10-Q09 already says "mix the cake".

problem: A caterpillar that becomes a butterfly makes a chrysalis; cocoons are made by moths.

fix.prompt: First the caterpillar eats. Then it makes a chrysalis. Then it becomes a butterfly.

evidence: Rule 11 (true content); life cycles are taught in primary science. Same fix as EN-LIS-T10-Q10.

problem: "cross" (UK for angry) can be read literally as the shape or as crossing the road, which other items in this bank use.

fix.prompt: Omar took three slow breaths when he felt angry. What did Omar do when he felt angry?

evidence: Rule 2 (literal language) and rule 12; "angry" is understood everywhere.

problem: The key "water helped her feel better" repeats "feel better" from the question, which no other option does, so it can be picked without reading.
evidence: Item-writing guidance: the key should not echo the stem (Haladyna, Downing & Rodriguez 2002).

problem: Exact duplicate of EN-RD-T15-Q09 (same text and question), and only the key repeats "probably" from the question.
evidence: A duplicate inflates practice of one item; the key echoing the stem is a giveaway (Haladyna et al. 2002). EN-RD-T15-Q09 keeps the content.

problem: The group label "not gentle" uses "not" in lower case.
evidence: Rule 9: NOT in capitals from level 3; a positive label is clearer still.

problem: The group "fun to say" is a matter of taste; "table" can be fun to say too.
evidence: A graded sort needs groups with one defensible answer (rule 10).

problem: The instruction asks "Why do you think that happened?" but the card asks "How did the boy feel?".

evidence: The instruction must match the question on the card (rule 2).

problem: "The boy's face lit up" is an idiom, and the inference depends on it.

fix.prompt: Ben noticed a boy standing alone. He walked over and asked him to play. The boy smiled. How did the boy feel?

evidence: Rule 2 (literal language); idioms are not the skill here (Vulchanova et al. 2015).

fix.instruction: Read the story. Answer the question.

fix.hint: Look at where the footprints go.
